examDifficulty.heading: How challenging is the Technical Architect Review Board?
examDifficulty.summary: The review board is the final CTA stage and a demanding architecture assessment. You receive an enterprise scenario, design a solution, present it, and defend your choices to a panel of Certified Technical Architects. There is no question paper or score for platform knowledge alone.
bullets: Live presentation and defence. Explain your architecture and answer detailed questions.
Practising CTA judges. The panel evaluates the areas required by the scenario.
Prerequisites apply. Hold both architect credentials and pass the evaluation first.
Fee: External sources report about US$4,500 for the board, separate from the evaluation. Confirm current pricing with Salesforce.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Candidates often prepare by completing several mock boards with practising CTAs. Practise presenting and defending a design aloud; platform knowledge by itself is not enough.

examFormat.heading: What happens at the Technical Architect Review Board?
examFormat.intro: The board is a scenario-based presentation followed by a defence. Prepare for these parts of the day:
bestWayToPass: Follow the same outline: Cover data, security and sharing, integration, delivery lifecycle, and licensing each time.
Start with the outcome: Explain the business result and overall solution before moving into technical details.
Raise risks early: Describe weak points and mitigations before the judges have to ask.
Practise interruptions: Rehearse answering challenges while keeping your reasoning clear.

practiceQuestionsIntroSuffix: , practise CTA-style reasoning and defending architecture decisions for the Review Board.

certificationCard.description: The final stage of CTA. You receive an enterprise scenario, design a full solution, then present and defend it to a panel of Certified Technical Architects. Passing earns the credential.

keyConcepts.h2: Technical Architect Review Board: preparation guide

blocks.heading: How the board works
blocks.body: You receive a scenario about a company, including its goals, systems, constraints, and problems. You prepare an architecture, present it to a panel, and answer extended questions. The judges test whether the solution meets the requirements, holds together, and can be defended under pressure. They are evaluating the required areas, not calculating a percentage score.

blocks.heading: Design for the stated needs
blocks.body: Address the scenario in front of you. Cover the data model and expected volume, record access for internal and external users, integrations and data direction, release practices, and licences. Prefer standard features where they fit and explain any custom work. Keep the design proportionate: every unnecessary component adds cost and creates another decision to defend.

blocks.heading: Present for a mixed audience
blocks.body: Explain the business outcome and solution outline first, then work through a consistent structure. Use diagrams that are readable and easy to discuss. Manage time so you reach each required area, including licensing and release management. Present in terms a business sponsor can follow; communication is part of the assessment.

blocks.heading: Respond to the panel
blocks.body: Expect questions that challenge choices or introduce new complications. For each important decision, know the requirement it supports, the alternative you rejected, and the trade-off you accepted. Reconsider a choice when an argument is sound; calmly defend it when your reasoning still holds. If you do not know something, say so and explain how you would find out rather than guessing.

blocks.heading: Common failure patterns
blocks.body: Candidates can miss stated requirements, include components they cannot justify, ignore trade-offs, or run out of time before covering every area. These problems reflect judgement and presentation as much as technical knowledge. A repeatable structure and full mock-board practice help expose them before the assessment.

scenarioTips.h2: How to prepare for the Technical Architect Review Board
scenarioTips.intro: The panel expects you to design within constraints and explain your choices when challenged. Practise the presentation and discussion, not only the technical topics.

blocks.heading: Use a consistent outline
blocks.body: Cover data, security and sharing, integration, delivery lifecycle, and licensing in the same order so you do not forget an area.

blocks.heading: Explain every component
blocks.body: For each item in the architecture, identify the requirement it serves and the alternative you considered.

blocks.heading: Raise risks and mitigations
blocks.body: Explain trade-offs yourself. Acknowledging limits shows that you assessed the design.

blocks.heading: Answer the challenge
blocks.body: Listen to the question and address it directly instead of repeating a prepared answer.

blocks.heading: Practise mock boards
blocks.body: Ask experienced architects to interrupt and question your decisions during rehearsal.

sampleQuestions.question: What happens during the Technical Architect Review Board?
options: Present and defend a scenario-based solution to a panel
Submit a written architecture document before the session
Complete a 60-question multiple-choice paper
Configure a solution in a live Salesforce org
sampleQuestions.explanation: The candidate presents an architecture and answers detailed questions from the panel.
whyWrong: A document alone is not the board assessment; the candidate must also defend the design.
The board does not use a multiple-choice paper.
The assessment is a presentation and discussion, not a live build.

sampleQuestions.question: A judge gives a sound reason to reconsider an integration choice. What should the candidate do?
options: Consider the objection and adjust when warranted
Keep the original design regardless of the objection
Ask the judge to make the architecture decision
Change the scenario requirement to fit the design
sampleQuestions.explanation: Considering a valid challenge and making a reasoned adjustment demonstrates judgement.
whyWrong: Ignoring a strong objection can appear inflexible.
The architect is responsible for evaluating options and making a recommendation.
The scenario requirements remain fixed; the design must address them.

sampleQuestions.question: A candidate runs out of time before discussing licensing and release management. Why is this a problem?
options: It is acceptable as long as the data model is detailed
The panel cannot assess required areas left uncovered
The judges will automatically cover both topics afterward
It changes the amount of the exam fee
sampleQuestions.explanation: The panel checks coverage of required areas. Missing topics because of poor time management creates gaps.
whyWrong: A strong data model does not replace other required areas.
Candidates are responsible for presenting the required coverage.
Fees are unrelated to the candidate’s performance.

sampleQuestions.question: What does the panel evaluate?
options: Speaking speed alone
Judgement, coverage, risk, and communication
The visual polish of the slide deck
Memory of feature names and platform limits only
sampleQuestions.explanation: The board focuses on how the candidate applies knowledge through sound decisions and clear communication.
whyWrong: Speed matters only when it affects clarity and coverage.
Clear visuals help, but slide polish is not the main criterion.
Prerequisite exams already assess platform knowledge; the board looks at architecture reasoning.

sampleQuestions.question: What must a candidate complete before taking the review board?
options: Employment at Salesforce
At least one relevant Trailhead superbadge
Both architect credentials and a passed evaluation
The Administrator credential alone
sampleQuestions.explanation: The CTA path requires both architect credentials, followed by a successful evaluation before the board.
whyWrong: There is no requirement to work for Salesforce.
A superbadge is not a CTA prerequisite.
Administrator alone does not meet the entry requirements.

sampleQuestions.question: A candidate cannot explain why an unneeded component appears in the design. What is the likely impact?
options: It demonstrates useful breadth without any downside
It raises the ambition score
It weakens the defence because every component needs a reason
It only uses presentation time and does not affect the assessment
sampleQuestions.explanation: A component the candidate cannot justify invites questions and undermines confidence in the overall design.
whyWrong: Extra components without a purpose add complexity rather than useful breadth.
Ambition is not the measure of architecture quality.
The panel assesses the reasoning, not only the time used.

sampleQuestions.question: How should a candidate begin the presentation?
options: List every Salesforce product included in the design
Lead with the business outcome and solution
Apologize for the time available before starting
Start by listing the governor limits that apply
sampleQuestions.explanation: Starting with the outcome helps the panel follow what the design is meant to achieve.
whyWrong: A product inventory does not establish the business value.
An apology uses time without explaining the design.
Technical limits are details, not the opening context.

sampleQuestions.question: The candidate is unsure about a product detail raised by a judge. What is the best response?
options: Invent an answer that sounds plausible
Blame the scenario for not explaining it
Admit uncertainty and explain how to verify
Switch to a stronger area of the design
sampleQuestions.explanation: It is better to be candid and explain how to find the answer than to make an unsupported claim.
whyWrong: Judges can recognize unsupported guesses, which harms credibility.
Blaming the scenario does not answer the question.
Avoiding the question is apparent to the panel.

sampleQuestions.question: Which issue commonly causes a candidate to fail the board?
options: A design that misses a stated requirement
Finishing before the allotted presentation time
Using standard Salesforce features where they fit
Knowing enterprise integration patterns in depth
sampleQuestions.explanation: Missing a stated requirement is a common and avoidable failure because requirement coverage is central to the assessment.
whyWrong: Time left over is acceptable if all required areas are covered.
Standard capabilities are often preferred when they meet the need.
Relevant architecture knowledge supports a stronger design.

sampleQuestions.question: Why should candidates use a consistent presentation outline?
options: It shortens the official session
It removes the need for architecture diagrams
State a trade-off and its mitigation
Cover each required area under time pressure
sampleQuestions.explanation: A repeatable order helps the candidate address data, security, integration, lifecycle, and licensing without relying on memory.
whyWrong: The allotted session length does not change.
Diagrams still help communicate the architecture.
The panel asks questions regardless of the presentation outline.

sampleQuestions.question: How should a candidate discuss trade-offs?
options: Avoid mentioning any weaknesses
List possible drawbacks without discussing a response
Explain the risk and how it will be managed
Claim the design has no disadvantages
sampleQuestions.explanation: Explaining a trade-off and how to manage it shows that the candidate has evaluated the design.
whyWrong: Unmentioned risks may emerge during questioning.
Identifying a drawback without considering mitigation leaves the analysis incomplete.
Every design has trade-offs; denying them suggests weak analysis.

sampleQuestions.question: Who evaluates the candidate at the review board?
options: Automated scoring software
Practising Certified Technical Architects
Sales representatives
Other candidates taking the board that day
sampleQuestions.explanation: The board is a live assessment by people who hold the CTA credential and practise architecture.
whyWrong: The decision is made by a panel, not automated software.
The board evaluates architecture rather than sales performance.
Candidates are assessed individually by the panel.

sampleQuestions.question: A solution uses custom code where a standard feature might work. What should the candidate do?
options: Remove the scenario requirement that prompted the design
Claim custom code is always more flexible
Present the code without explaining the choice
Justify custom work or use the standard feature
sampleQuestions.explanation: Custom work needs a reason; if standard capability meets the requirement, it is usually the better choice.
whyWrong: The stated requirements cannot be removed.
Flexibility by itself does not justify maintenance and complexity.
Unexplained choices are likely to be challenged.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the most useful preparation for the panel’s questions?
options: Practise defending designs in mock boards
Read more documentation without presenting a design
Create longer slides for the presentation
Memorize the scenario format
sampleQuestions.explanation: Mock boards build the skill of explaining and defending decisions during live questioning.
whyWrong: Documentation supports platform knowledge but does not rehearse live defence.
Longer slides reduce time for discussion and do not practise responses.
Knowing the format alone does not prepare the candidate to defend choices.

sampleQuestions.question: How does the panel reach its decision?
options: Through automated scoring with no human review
By counting the candidate’s years of experience
Using a percentage score from multiple-choice answers
Panel judgement against the scenario requirements
sampleQuestions.explanation: The panel evaluates the candidate’s architecture and defence against the scenario; it is not a percentage-based question score.
whyWrong: The panel makes the decision.
Experience can help preparation but does not determine the outcome.
There is no multiple-choice answer sheet.
